\chapter{Synthesis --- More Than One}
\label{ch:synthesis-more-than-one}
\hlchaptermodality{77}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can contrast a bare plural with a definite plural, and know that the indefinite article is dropped rather than pluralised.}

Complete ES-C44-sintesis-mas-de-uno: say tengo libros and tengo los libros and explain what separates them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — more than one}

\label{lesson:ES-C44-sintesis-mas-de-uno}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I have a book.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Tengo un libro}.) Now say \textquotedblleft{}I have books,\textquotedblright{} and notice where you hesitate.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the article that leaves}]
The hesitation is the right instinct. \emph{The} pluralised neatly — \emph{el} became \emph{los}. \emph{A} cannot, because \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}more than one\textquotedblright{} disagree by definition.

English solves this by swapping in another word: \emph{a book} $\to$ \emph{some books}, or just \emph{books}. Spanish takes the shorter road:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Tengo \textbf{un} libro.} — I have a book. \emph{Tengo libro\textbf{s}.} — I have books.
\end{quote}

\textbf{The article simply goes.} Not replaced, not pluralised — dropped. A bare plural noun is a complete, ordinary Spanish phrase.

This is the mirror image of everything you have been doing. For fifty chapters Spanish has made you say \emph{more} than English: two genders, four articles, six verb endings. Here, for once, it says less.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Read this aloud and watch the two plurals doing different jobs.

\begin{quote}
— \emph{¿Tienes libros?} — \emph{Sí, tengo libros.} — \emph{¿Y los libros de la casa?} — \emph{Los libros de la casa, no.}
\end{quote}

Bare \emph{libros} means \textquotedblleft{}books, some books, books in general.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Los libros} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the} books\textquotedblright{} — particular ones, already known to both of you.

That is the same distinction English makes and never explains: \emph{do you have books?} is a different question from \emph{do you have the books?} You have simply never had to choose it deliberately before.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tengo un libro\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Tengo libros\textquotedblright{} — hear the article vanish
  \item \textquotedblleft{}libros\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}los libros\textquotedblright{}, twice, until the two feel like different questions
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}I have books\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Tengo libros}} — no article.) \textquotedblleft{}I have the books\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Tengo los libros}}.) Which article pluralises and which one leaves? (\textbf{The} pluralises; \textbf{a} leaves.) Next: the small words that let you stop naming a thing you have already named.
\end{tcolorbox}
